analysis.subject: earth-science
analysis.pageCoverage: Page covers simple equator-to-pole flow without rotation and the actual three-cell circulation with pressure bands and weather belts.

overview.headline: Three atmospheric cells that shape pressure belts and global weather patterns

keyPoints.point: Global circulation is the movement of air around the planet that transports thermal energy.
keyPoints.quote: Global Atmospheric Circulation is the movement of air around the planet.

keyPoints.point: Without rotation warm air would move directly north toward the poles and sink to create high pressure.
keyPoints.quote: That warm air would then move directly north toward the poles, where it would become very cold and sink, creating a large area of high pressure.

keyPoints.point: Earth rotation creates easterly movement of air called the Coriolis effect that breaks up simple circulation.
keyPoints.quote: The Earth’s rotation results in an easterly-movement of air, called the Coriolis effect

keyPoints.point: Instead of one large circulation each hemisphere contains three circulations of air that form distinct cells.
keyPoints.quote: Instead of one large circulation in each hemisphere, there are three circulations in each:

keyTerms.gloss: Low latitude convection cell where air near the equator is heated and rises vertically.
keyTerms.quote: Hadley cell – At low latitudes, air moves toward the equator, where it is heated and rises vertically.

keyTerms.gloss: Mid latitude cell where surface air flows poleward and eastward through friction.
keyTerms.quote: Ferrel cell – In this mid-latitude atmospheric circulation cell, air near the surface flows poleward and eastward

keyTerms.gloss: Smallest high latitude cell where air rises and travels toward the cold poles.
keyTerms.quote: Polar cell – At higher latitudes, air rises and travels toward the poles.

keyTerms.gloss: Apparent shift from Earth rotation that causes easterly movement of air.
keyTerms.quote: The Earth’s rotation results in an easterly-movement of air, called the Coriolis effect

keyTerms.gloss: Belt of sinking air around 30° N/S latitude at each pole linked to fair dry weather.
keyTerms.quote: The high pressure band is located at about 30° N/S latitude and at each pole.

componentPlan.pedagogicalReason: Builds the three cells in page order so students see how low, mid and polar flows link.
componentPlan.focusQuote: Instead of one large circulation in each hemisphere, there are three circulations in each:

componentPlan.pedagogicalReason: Helps students sort high and low pressure bands by latitude to connect circulation to desert and storm belts.
componentPlan.focusQuote: Between each of these circulation cells are surface-level bands of high and low pressure.
